title: The first working dubhan
body: Dubhan makes a fuel without the vein, rough but good to burn. It is no trade yet. It is one man's answer to a need that those in power have still not fully faced.

title: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's note on the fuel
body: At the foot of the year the royal chronicler writes that a fuel made without the vein is reported from the north, and that she has not seen it. Hers is the first mention of dubhan in the royal record, and she spells the word three ways in two lines.

title: The Board's inquiry
body: The Mine Board sends two surveyors north to learn whether the new fuel burns as men say. Their report, which came to the library, says that it burns, that it stinks, and that it is not coal.

title: The lamp-houses of the capital
body: The street-lamps of Cathair dhearg, which have burned coal since the humans set them up, are left dark in the poorer streets to save fuel. When dubhan comes, the dark streets are the first lit again.

title: The last coal sale at the fair
body: The court of the fair at Muileann òg records its last sale of coal-fuel by the cartload. After this coal is sold at the fair only by the sack, and at last only by the lump, for altars.

title: Cathal crowned
body: Mairead's reign ends while Dubhan's first trials still fail more than they succeed. Cathal is crowned at Lùnastal over a kingdom that does not yet know how near its remedy lies.

title: The mint's new dies
body: The mint at Cathair dhearg cuts new dies for the coinage of the reign. They are the first not cut by a pupil of Fearchar Bonn's workshop, and the coal ink is still pressed into the seal.

title: The shipmasters' works at Seann Skell
body: A company of shipmasters sets up a works for the making of dubhan at Seann Skell on the southern coast, the first on the island outside the north. On what terms they had the making of it is not told.

title: The high custodian's letter
body: The Àrd-choimheadaiche at Seann Skell writes to every house of the Rite that the new fuel is not forbidden, since it is not coal, and not blessed, since it is not coal. The letter is read in the houses and argued in the druid schools for years.

title: The Seann Skell works' first year
body: The dubhan works at Seann Skell on the southern coast sell their first year's making to the fishing boats of the south coast and the lamp-houses of Cathair dhearg. The works' chimney is the tallest thing on the coast.

title: Peigi nic Ascaill's trial lamp
body: Peigi nic Ascaill, engineer to the Lighthouse Board, fits a dubhan burner to a spare lamp in the yard below Taigh-solais Baile ìseal and runs it for a hundred nights. Murchadh mac Coinnich, retired from the light, keeps the log of the trial for her.

title: The fishing boats of Caol fhiadhaich
body: The boatwrights of Caol fhiadhaich on the south-west coast fit dubhan engines to the first fishing boats. The Shipwrights' Guild calls the work unlawful for its members. The boatwrights leave the guild and keep the work.

title: The shipwrights' guild court
body: The court of the Shipwrights' Guild at Ros dhomhain rules that the fitting of an engine is no shipwright's work and so outside its charter. The boatwrights of Caol fhiadhaich are readmitted to the guild. They decline.

title: The lights turned to dubhan
body: The five beacons of the coast, which have burned coal-lit flame for more than a century, are the first works of the kingdom turned by order to dubhan.

title: The last coal flame
body: The coal flame of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg is borne in a closed lantern to the Rite's house at Seann Skell and let burn out on the altar. Custodians from four shires attend, and Ciorstaidh nic Artair, keeper of the light, carries the lantern.

title: Taigh-solais Muileann bheag converted
body: The beacon at Muileann bheag on the Tuathaich north coast is turned to dubhan with the others. Its fuel is carted from the north; of the five lights it alone is not fed by sea from Seann Skell.

title: Taigh-solais Àth dhearg converted
body: At Taigh-solais Àth dhearg on the north-east cape the work takes a month longer than at the others, for the stair is too narrow for the new tank. The tank is lifted to the lamp-room from outside by a crane borrowed from the rope-walk at Seann Tarr.

title: Taigh-solais Baile chrom converted
body: At Taigh-solais Baile chrom on the Tuathaich coast the work is done by Tuathaich fitters from Caol mhòr, for the Lighthouse Board has none of its own to send so far. The keeper's report names none of them.

title: The lamp-makers turn
body: The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin begin to make dubhan lamps and ask leave to set their guild mark on them. After a year's argument the guild court allows it. The flame over the hammer is kept.

title: Daniel Frayne dies
body: Daniel Frayne, speaker of the Moot, dies at Muileann leathan. The Moot chooses Martha Greaves of Doire ghlas, a mill manager, to follow him.

title: The binders of Muileann leathan
body: The Moot sends Daniel Frayne's pupils, the binders of Muileann leathan, to rebind its minute-books from the first meeting. The rebound set is kept at Caol mhòr. A second set is made and hidden, says the Moot's minute, elsewhere.

title: The coal line's first dubhan engine
body: The Rail Board runs its first dubhan engine on the coal line, from the yards at Muileann chrom to Cathair dhearg. It carries no coal. It carries dubhan to the lamp-houses of the capital, and comes back empty.

title: The eastern salt-road
body: For the first time salt from Àth bheag goes to the inland towns by dubhan lorry, on the drove road past Baile ìseal. Within a few years the drovers of the east coast sell their oxen.

title: Achadh mhòr's drovers
body: The drovers of Achadh mhòr in the south, with no oxen left to drive, buy lorries. The drove-inn at An Sligeanach Fad' às keeps its trade by selling them dubhan.

title: The inns take the new lamps
body: The inns along the old mining roads hang dubhan lamps. In a single decade the oil and the wick, which lit them for centuries, are gone.

title: An Leòmhann Buidhe keeps a wick
body: At An Leòmhann Buidhe on the north-east road the landlord keeps one wick lamp burning over the door beside the new dubhan lamps. The custom spreads along the roads, and a wick lamp over an inn door is still called a Leòmhann.

title: The first horseless carriage
body: Fitters at Seann Skell on the southern coast set a lorry's dubhan engine under a closed carriage for the high custodian of the Rite. It is the first carriage on the island that needs no horse. Within a few years the council and the Mine Board have them too.

title: Am Buabhall Fortanach
body: Am Buabhall Fortanach, the tavern on the south-west road near Doire shean, is the last of the great inns to hang dubhan lamps. Its landlady's account-book gives the cost as a year's takings.

title: The Taigh-seinnse Mòr's hall
body: An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, on the old coal road above Cuan chrom, opens a second hall lit wholly by dubhan. It is let for weddings, wakes and the meetings of the Guild of Hewers, whose own hall at Achadh dhomhain has been sold.

title: An Taigh-òsta Grianach
body: An Taigh-òsta Grianach, on the south-east road near Cnoc dhìreach, is rebuilt with dubhan lamps in every room and a dubhan pump at the door. It is the first inn on the island to sell fuel as well as beds.

title: The coal engines laid up
body: The Rail Board's coal-fired engines are laid up in a siding at Muileann chrom and never run again. The yard families who drove them are taught the dubhan engines, such of them as will learn.

title: An Taigh-seinnse Reòta
body: An Taigh-seinnse Reòta on the north road above Muileann fhada is the last of the great inns to keep a wick lamp in every room. Its landlord writes to the Board that the reek of dubhan drives away his guests. It does not, and the next year he puts in the lamps.

title: Muileann dhearg closed
body: The last working face under Muileann dhearg is shut. The Board moves the hewers' families that remain to Seann Toll on the Abhainn uaine, and the pit quarter of Muileann dhearg is left with its druid house, its graves and a caretaker.

title: The Muileann dhearg families at Seann Toll
body: The families from Muileann dhearg are settled in a new row at the edge of Seann Toll, which the town calls the Hewers' Row. Few of them find work on the boats. Most work at the dubhan tanks by the river landing.

title: Muileann dhearg's druid house
body: The druid house at Muileann dhearg is given to the town's caretaker to keep, with the graves. Once a year the druid school at Caol shean sends a teacher to give the town's one remaining lecture, and few come.

title: The word spreads before the fuel does
body: Men begin to say "dubhan" for the fuel itself, as well as for the man who made it, years before the trade built upon it is whole.

title: Dubhan-tùsail
body: The word 'dubhan-tùsail' is first found in a letter of the druid school at Caol shean. It is used of a first attempt that seemed a dead end and proved otherwise, and the letter uses it of the school's own revival.

title: The Rail Board's new name
body: In its own timetables the Rail Board drops 'coal' from the name of its main line and calls it only the line. Everyone else still calls it the coal line.

title: The Guild of Hewers dissolved
body: The Guild of Hewers, chartered at Achadh dhomhain in the first years of the restored custom, dissolves itself. Its rolls, its oath-stone of coal and its sick-roll go to the library. Its last master, Tormod mac Dhonnchaidh, writes that the guild had outlived the mountain's patience.

title: The bath-house given to the Rite
body: The bath-house at the hot springs near Muileann ruadh, built by the Hewers for their sick, passes with the guild's other goods to the custodians of the Rite. It is opened to any who pay, and for the first time to the Tuathaich.

title: The Achadh dhomhain hall
body: The Hewers' hall at Achadh dhomhain, sold before the guild was dissolved, becomes a dubhan depot. Its carved lintel, with the guild's oath cut in it, is left in its place above the pumps.

title: The trade turns to dubhan
body: Markets, the supply of the host and the shipping turn wholly to the new fuel. The coal caste sees the source of its own power fail, and makes no objection.

title: Buses and hired cars
body: Dubhan buses begin to run between Cathair dhearg, Inis mhòr and Cathair mhòr, and hired cars wait at the bridge in the capital. Dia-thìris takes the names of both from the humans' tongue as it found them, bus and tacsaidh; for the engine and the train it had made words of its own.

title: The house of Mac Ùisdein moves
body: The house of Mac Ùisdein sells what is left of its share in the spoil and quarry of the Sloc Mòr and puts its money into dubhan shipping at Ros dhomhain. Of the families that held the vein it alone moves before the vein fails it.

title: The fleet's first dubhan hulls
body: The kingdom's patrol boats at Ros dhomhain are refitted for dubhan, and for the first time they can outrun the raiders. The next two raider hulks taken are brought into Ros dhomhain under tow.

title: Raiders taken to Ros dhomhain
body: The crews of the raider hulks brought into Ros dhomhain are tried at the court of the sea there. Several of them are Tuathaich. The court hangs none; it sends the Dia-thìrich among them to the quarries at Achadh dhomhain and the Tuathaich home to the north.

title: The Fuel-Fitters chartered
body: The fitters of dubhan engines, who have worked outside every guild, are chartered as the Guild of Fuel-Fitters at Seann Skell on the southern coast. Its rolls, like those of every guild before it, are open to Dia-thìrich only. The Tuathaich fitters already in the trade are let go.

title: Tuathaich fitters go north
body: The fitters let go under the charter rule go back to the northern towns and fit engines there without a guild. Within a few years the harbour of Caol mhòr holds more dubhan boats than any port of its size in the south.

title: The Moot on the new fuel
body: The Moot at Caol mhòr, under Martha Greaves, debates whether the north shall take up the new fuel or keep to its own seams. It votes to take it up. The delegates of the western pit towns walk out.

title: The Tuathaich depots
body: Dubhan depots are opened at Caol mhòr, Doire ghlas and Ceann mhòr, supplied by sea. Martha Greaves writes in the Moot's minute that the north now buys its fire from the south, and does not say whether this is good.

title: The fourth currency reform
body: For the first time the coin of the Rìoghachd is pegged to the making of dubhan and not to the stores of coal. So the kingdom owns, quietly, which of the two now runs it.

title: The Dubhan Era proclaimed
body: At the same sitting the council proclaims that the Age of the Kingdom ended with the first working dubhan, and that the kingdom's years are counted anew from that day. The year is entered as the fifteenth of the Dubhan Era. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh re-heads fourteen years of her chronicle, and writes at the foot of the page that never before has she had to move a year she was living in.

title: The plain seal
body: The mint at Cathair dhearg ceases to press coal ink into the seal of the coinage. The new seal is plain. Fearchar Bonn's first dies are given to the library and kept in the case beside the oath-stone of the Guild of Hewers.

title: The Rite's protest on the seal
body: The high custodian at Seann Skell protests to the council that the plain seal is a sign the kingdom no longer holds the vein sacred. The council answers that the kingdom never said it did. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh copies both letters into the chronicle.

title: The western pit towns meet
body: Delegates of the western pit towns meet at Muileann àrsaidh, apart from the Moot. They agree to go on working their seams and to sell their coal to any household in the north that will buy it.

title: Àth naomh joins the pit towns
body: Àth naomh, a Tuathaich town of the western hills with only a few old shafts, joins the pit towns' agreement. Its delegates say the town would sooner be cold with its neighbours than warm alone.

title: The northern towns hold out
body: A number of northern towns will not go over to the new fuel. They work the last good coal seams sooner than trade their freedom for need of one man's fuel.

title: The holdout towns
body: Chief among the towns that refuse are five of the western hills: Àth leathan, Muileann àrsaidh, Cnoc thais, Àth naomh and Tobar dhearg. Their spokeswoman is Ruth Calder, a pit captain's daughter of Àth leathan. The Moot at Caol mhòr neither joins them nor condemns them.

title: Tom Varley's pits
body: At Cnoc thais the pit captain Tom Varley opens again two shafts that have lain abandoned since the humans' time. The coal is poor. It is theirs, and it warms the town.

title: Tobar dhearg of the hills
body: Tobar dhearg in the western hills, least of the holdout towns, has one pit and forty hewers. It sends its coal to Cathair gheal on the coast and has fish in return.

title: Ellen Marsh's books
body: Ellen Marsh, a schoolteacher of Doire ghlas, finishes her gathering of Tuathaich accounts of the Severance and the settlement, taken down over many years from the old folk of the north. It fills eleven books. It is her request that goes to the library.

title: The library's Tuathaich wing proposed
body: A request is laid before Leabharlann Muileann chaol that the Tuathaich tellings be kept beside the Dia-thìrich record. It is laid on the table and not refused, and there it lies to this day.

title: The keeper's answer
body: Raghnall mac Mhuirich answers Ellen Marsh that the request awaits the council's view on the standing of spoken witness. The council has given none.

title: Ellen Marsh's reply
body: Ellen Marsh writes back to the keeper that spoken witness was good enough for the census clerks when they took the Moot's figures. Her letter is filed with the request.

title: The coal price in the north
body: The holdout pits sell their coal to Tuathaich households across the north for less than the price of dubhan. The Moot's own wool mills at Doire ghlas buy it. For the first time since the Severance the Board's takings from the north fall.

title: The Board's northern revenue
body: The Mine Board's accounts show its northern takings down by a quarter. Its report to the council names the western pits as the cause and the Leòid ruling as the remedy.

title: The seams declared Crown property
body: Under the Leòid ruling the Mine Board declares the western seams the Crown's, holding that the right to work them lapsed when the holders ceased to pay the fifth. The holders say they ceased to pay when the Board ceased to carry the coal. The pits are ordered shut.

title: Enforcers posted to the west
body: A company of the Board's enforcers is posted at Seann Skell in the west to shut the pits. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh notes that it is the first armed company the kingdom has sent toward the north since the Severance.

title: The enforcers' depot
body: The enforcers at Seann Skell in the west build a dubhan depot for their lorries at the edge of the town. The town's house of Manannan will not bless it, and the high custodian of the Rite sends a priest to bless it instead.

title: The Moot's warning
body: Martha Greaves writes to the council from Caol mhòr that the western towns will not shut their pits for a letter, and asks a year's delay while the Moot treats with them. The letter is received and filed.

title: First skirmishes
body: Small fights begin between the state's enforcers and the Tuathaich who hold to their coal. None is written down, and none is great enough to name; together they lead straight into open war.

title: The chronicler asks
body: At the foot of the year Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh writes that fighting is reported in the west, that the Board's reports of it are not given to the chronicler, and that she has asked for them. They were not given.

title: The pit-heads walled
body: The pit-heads at Muileann àrsaidh are walled with spoil and timber, and the road into the town from the south is dug across. The Board's enforcers at Seann Skell report the town shut against them.

title: Ruth Calder's letter
body: Ruth Calder writes to the council for the western towns. She offers to pay the Crown's fifth in coal if the Board will carry it and let the pits work until the seams are spent. The letter came to the library. No answer to it did.

title: The Moot stands apart
body: The Moot at Caol mhòr resolves that it is no party to the quarrel of the Board and the western towns, and that it will feed any who come hungry to its towns. The resolution is carried by nine votes.

title: The Moot's granaries
body: The Moot orders its granaries at Caol mhòr and Doire ghlas filled beyond the wont, paying from the takings of the wool mills. The minute gives no reason.

title: Sìleas nic Rath
body: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh lays down the office, and Sìleas nic Rath, her clerk, becomes royal chronicler. Hers is the record of the war that the library afterwards seals.

title: The regiments called up
body: Regiments not called to arms since the Severance itself are formed and armed anew, openly, months before any in power will own that war is coming.

title: Somhairle mac Lachlainn
body: Command of the new-formed regiments is given to Somhairle mac Lachlainn, who rose among the Board's enforcers. The rolls of the Severance companies are brought out of the council's chests at Cathair dhearg to name the regiments, and the old names are read aloud before new men.

title: The Moot's last petition
body: On Christmas Day Martha Greaves carries a petition of the Moot in person to the council at Cathair dhearg. It asks that the western pits be let work out their seams, which the Moot says will be spent in a few years whatever is done. It is received and filed. She is the first speaker of the Moot to enter the council chamber.

title: Arms by the coal line
body: The Rail Board carries arms and dubhan from Cathair dhearg to Seann Bhral on the coal line and its western branch. The yard at Muileann chrom works day and night on the trains.

title: The hewers gather at Àth leathan
body: Hewers of the five western towns gather at Àth leathan, where the road from the south enters the hills. The Board's lists name Ruth Calder and Tom Varley among them.

title: The regiments go west
body: The regiments set out from Cathair dhearg by the western road, their carts and lorries running on dubhan, to join the enforcers at Seann Skell in the west.

title: Battle of Àth leathan
body: The first great battle of An Cogadh Fada, the Long War. The state, whose failing power already leans on Dubhan's fuel, moves against the holdouts in arms.

title: The dead of Àth leathan
body: The open record counts the kingdom's dead at Àth leathan and not the holdouts'. The Tuathaich tellings put theirs in the hundreds. After this battle Ruth Calder's name is not found in the open record.

title: Into the hills
body: After Àth leathan the holdouts give up the southern pits and fall back into the hills about Muileann àrsaidh and Cnoc thais. The pits at Àth leathan are taken without a fight and flooded by the Board's order.

title: An seachdamh rèisimeid raised
body: The seventh regiment is raised from the levies of the west coast and stationed at Seann Skell, the river port nearest the western hills. It holds the road behind the army and the field of Àth leathan.

title: The field of Àth leathan after
body: The field of Àth leathan is left unploughed. The patrols of the seventh regiment pass it on the road to the western hills and report it empty.

title: The wartime tithe
body: For the war a tax is laid, for a time, on every sale of dubhan in the kingdom. It is never lifted after the war ends.

title: The tithe at the pumps
body: The wartime tithe is taken at the dubhan depots, where a clerk of the Treasury sits beside every pump. Within a month the fair-court at Muileann òg records the first complaint against it.

title: A' chiad rèisimeid raised
body: The first regiment is raised at Inis mhòr, the river port beside the capital, from the capital's own companies. It guards the council, the mint and the bridge over the Abhainn dhomhain.

title: A' chiad chabhlach raised
body: The first fleet is raised from the south-west harbours and stationed at Àth gharbh, its hulls lying in the harbour of Doire shean a short walk away. It is sent round the western cape to stop the coal going out by sea from the Tuathaich ports.

title: An ceathramh cabhlach raised
body: The fourth fleet is raised at Cuan shean on the west coast and joins the first off the Tuathaich shore. Between them they close Seann Skell and Cnoc bhàn in the north-west to every boat but fishing boats, and search those.

title: The siege of Muileann àrsaidh
body: The regiments lay siege to Muileann àrsaidh. The town holds for weeks on stored coal and potatoes, and its pit-heads are taken one by one. Sìleas nic Rath's open record gives the day it fell and nothing else.

title: An treas rèisimeid raised
body: The third regiment is raised at Cathair mhòr, where the Mine Board keeps its offices in the old stone house of Mac Ùisdein. Its first muster is held under the market cross the house raised.

title: An còigeamh rèisimeid raised
body: The fifth regiment is raised at Seann Warr on the lake shore west of the capital. It is sent north to relieve the regiments before Muileann àrsaidh.

title: The capital's lamp-houses rationed
body: Dubhan for the army is taken before every other use. The poorer streets of the capital go dark again, as they were before the fuel came, and the lamp-houses of Cathair dhearg ration it street by street.

title: Families at Caol mhòr
body: Families from the western pits come into Caol mhòr and Doire ghlas with what they can carry. The Moot feeds them from its own stores, as it resolved to do. The council sends nothing and forbids nothing.

title: The Moot's granaries opened
body: The Moot opens its granaries at Caol mhòr and Doire ghlas to the families from the west. Its minute records how much was given and the names of the families; it is one of the few Tuathaich records of the war that the library does not hold.

title: Agnes Pike's school as a shelter
body: The school at Doire ghlas that Agnes Pike founded is given over to the families from the west, and its benches serve for beds. Ellen Marsh, who teaches there, takes down the families' accounts.

title: Cnoc thais taken
body: Cnoc thais is taken after the regiments cut the road to its pits. Tom Varley's two shafts are fired and sealed. The open record gives the number of holdouts taken, and not the number who went on into the hills.

title: Onto the windy coast
body: Some of the holdouts of Cnoc thais go on beyond the hills and out onto the windy coast of the far north-west. The regiments follow them to the edge of the shire of Seann Vell and no farther. The open record names them, as it names every foe of the war, only as those 'of no shire'.

title: An dàrna cabhlach raised
body: The second fleet is raised at Seann Skell on the southern coast, to keep the eastern and southern waters while the first and fourth are in the north-west.

title: Raiders take the salt-boats
body: With the fleets drawn to the north-west, raiders from the eastern waters take two salt-boats off Àth bheag and burn a third. The second fleet runs down one of the raiders off Baile ìseal.

title: An siathamh rèisimeid raised
body: The sixth regiment is raised at Cnoc bheag, the great river port of the Hawk houses in the north-central country. It holds the northern road between the Tuathaich shires and the middle of the island, and the Hawk houses bless its colours by their own rite.

title: An dàrna rèisimeid raised
body: The second regiment is raised at Àth dhìreach in the east and set to guard the coal line and the library road. Its camp is the first soldiery the town of Muileann chaol has seen.

title: An ceathramh rèisimeid raised
body: The fourth regiment is raised at Caol bheag in the north-east. It goes down the Abhainn ghorm to Ros chiar, is shipped west round the north coast in hired dubhan hulls, and is landed at Ceann mhòr in the Tuathaich north.

title: The regiments at Ceann mhòr
body: The fourth regiment is quartered at Ceann mhòr, in the old human magistrate's house that the maor has kept since the shires were drawn. The Moot protests the quartering. The protest is received.

title: The fishermen of Cathair gheal
body: The fleets off the north-west search the fishing boats of Cathair gheal on every day they put out. The fishermen petition the Moot, and the Moot petitions the council. The searching goes on.

title: An t-ochdamh rèisimeid raised
body: The eighth regiment is raised at Inis uaine on the Abhainn chaol in the east, to guard the dubhan depots and tanks of the eastern ports, which the council fears the holdouts may fire.

title: An treas cabhlach raised
body: The third fleet is raised at Baile ghorm on the south-west coast, and carries the army's dubhan up the west coast in tank-hulls to the regiments in the hills.

title: The Baile chrom vigil
body: The Grey Night sect at Baile chrom keeps its vigil as always. The regiments quartered along the coast report a night when the whole town was dark and silent; they search it, and find nothing.

title: Àth naomh and Tobar dhearg
body: The last two western towns, Àth naomh and Tobar dhearg, open their roads to the regiments without a siege. Their pits are flooded. The open record names no holdouts taken at either.

title: An naoidheamh rèisimeid raised
body: The ninth regiment is raised at Seann Skell on the southern coast, the second town of that name in the regimental list, to guard the dubhan works the shipmasters built there. The regimental clerks tell the two apart by river and coast.

title: The column goes south
body: A column of holdouts, some hundreds strong, leaves the western hills and marches south-east through the middle of the island toward the capital. Why it did so is in the sealed archive. The Tuathaich tellings name its leader Owen Barrow. The open record gives no name.

title: The column's road
body: The column's road south-east runs by Àth bheag in the west, Muileann mhin and the edge of the capital's country. The towns it passes report it, and the open record copies their reports and not the regiments'.

title: The camp by Muileann ghlas
body: The column passes Muileann òg and camps on the fields by Muileann ghlas, a day's walk from Cathair dhearg. The first and third regiments are brought down the fair road to meet it.

title: The fair-ground emptied
body: The fair-ground at Muileann òg is cleared of its standing booths to give the first and third regiments room to camp. The books of its court for that year end with no closing entry.

title: Battle of Muileann ghlas
body: The second great battle of the war, and the last. In two summers of fighting the Tuathaich holdouts are broken: children of the humans once driven to the island's edge, driven back again, and this time by a fuel that one of their own devised.

title: The field at Muileann ghlas
body: The open record lists the first and third regiments on the field at Muileann ghlas and gives no count of the column's dead. The regiments' own dead are named on a stone at Cathair mhòr, set up the next year.

title: The last pits give up
body: Word of Muileann ghlas reaches the hills, and the holdouts still there come down to the posts of the seventh regiment on the Àth leathan road. They are disarmed and sent home. The open record counts their weapons.

title: An Cogadh Fada ends
body: The Long War ends. Nine regiments and four fleets were raised in it, each named for the town where it is stationed, and all of them stand to this day.

title: Fadachadh
body: Among Tuathaich speakers 'chaidh am fadachadh', they got long-warred, begins to be said of the defeat in the west, and then of any defeat after holding out too long. It is said as a jest, and those who say it do not laugh.

title: The regiments stay on their stations
body: The nine regiments and four fleets are not stood down. The council keeps each at the town where it was raised and pays them from the wartime tithe.

title: The market charter of Caol ruadh
body: Caol ruadh, whose harbour victualled the garrisons and the second fleet through the war, is granted a market right for the southern strait. It is the sixteenth market town, and the last chartered.

title: Dubhan's fuel over all the island
body: With the last ordered resistance gone, Dubhan's fuel is in all but law compelled upon the whole trade of the island.

title: The western seams flooded
body: By the Board's order the last western seams are flooded and their shafts capped with concrete. The seventh regiment stands by at every capping. After this no coal is dug on the island outside the Board's own works.

title: The prisoners sent home
body: The holdouts held since Muileann ghlas are let out of the capital's gaol and sent north under guard of the first regiment as far as the boundary stones. The Moot's register adds their names, in a column of their own, to the dead and maimed it has kept since the Severance.

title: Somhairle mac Lachlainn seated
body: Somhairle mac Lachlainn is given a seat on the council, the first soldier to sit there since the captains of the Severance war.

title: The seventh regiment at Àth leathan
body: The seventh regiment builds a post on the road below Àth leathan and keeps a company there. In the regimental lists it is called the Àth leathan post, and in the town something else.

title: The stone at Cathair mhòr
body: A stone is set up at Cathair mhòr bearing the names of the regiments' dead from Àth leathan and Muileann ghlas. It stands beside the market cross of the house of Mac Ùisdein.

title: The Muileann ghlas field
body: The field at Muileann ghlas where the column camped is sown again. For years the farmer who holds it finds weapons in the furrows and hands them to the first regiment, which keeps a list.

title: The library's war archive sealed
body: The whole record of the Long War at Leabharlann Muileann chaol is sealed against all readers for fifty years. No other archive in the kingdom's history has been sealed.

title: Sìleas nic Rath's open chronicle
body: Of the royal chronicle for the war years there stays open only Sìleas nic Rath's list of places, the regiments present and the counts she was allowed. Her full record went into the sealed archive with the rest.

title: The cairn at Àth leathan
body: Tuathaich families build a cairn on the field of Àth leathan without leave. The patrols of the seventh regiment leave it standing, and every time they pass it has grown by a stone or two.

title: The tithe carried forward
body: The Treasury's accounts carry the wartime tithe forward as a standing line under the regiments' pay. No minute of the council records a choice to keep it.

title: The market-due fixed
body: The Treasury fixes the market-due at seventeen in the hundred on every sale a town makes into its market and on every sale between markets. A clerk of the Treasury is set in each of the sixteen market towns to take it and keep the market roll. The wartime tithe on dubhan stays at the pumps, on its own line.

title: The Fuel-Fitters and the regiments
body: The Guild of Fuel-Fitters at Seann Skell on the southern coast is given the contract for the regiments' engines and the fleets' hulls, and doubles its rolls. The charter rule holds, and all its new fitters are Dia-thìrich.

title: The regiments' arms contracts
body: The forges of Àth naomh in the west and Caol ìseal on the north coast, which smelt the bog-iron of their districts, take the Crown's contract for the regiments' small arms and field-guns. The forge-towns of the old vein country follow. Arms become the dearest common goods in every market of the kingdom.

title: The second fleet off Baile ìseal
body: The second fleet runs down off Baile ìseal the raiders who took the salt-boats in the war, and brings their hulls into Seann Skell. The lighthouse log at Baile ìseal records the chase from the lamp-room.

title: The fourth fleet in the north-west
body: The fourth fleet, kept on the Tuathaich coast after the war, searches the raiders' bays off Cathair gheal and finds them empty. The fishermen of Cathair gheal say the raiders left when the fleets came and will return when they go.

title: The third fleet's tank-hulls
body: The third fleet at Baile ghorm keeps its tank-hulls after the war and runs dubhan up the west coast to the Tuathaich depots on the council's contract. The Moot pays the freight.

title: The creature off the cape again
body: The fourth fleet's log for the year records a thing longer than a patrol boat off the north-west cape, where the Tuathaich fishermen reported one in Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill's day. The log calls it a whale.

title: Anna nic Phàil's motion
body: The motion to make amends to the Tuathaich is brought into the council by Anna nic Phàil, councillor for Cathair dhomhain, on a petition of the Moot under Martha Greaves. She speaks for it once.

title: The motion for amends
body: In the capital it is proposed to pay the Tuathaich for their losses in the war. The motion is let die quietly, and no vote is taken.

title: The Moot's minute on the amends
body: The Moot's minute on the motion for amends runs to one line: 'Allowed to die.' That same year Martha Greaves lays down the chair. The Moot chooses Peter Hale, a great-grandson of its first speaker, to follow her.

title: The fifth regiment's barracks
body: The fifth regiment builds stone barracks at Seann Warr, the first lasting quarters any of the nine regiments has had. The town gives the land and takes the regiment's custom.

title: The eighth regiment at Inis uaine
body: The eighth regiment's guard on the eastern dubhan tanks at Inis uaine is made lasting. Its officers take houses in the town, and the Seann Spioradan house of Inis uaine adds the regiment to its prayers.

title: The fourth regiment leaves Ceann mhòr
body: The fourth regiment leaves the old magistrate's house at Ceann mhòr and goes home to Caol bheag. The Moot asks that the house be given to the town. It is given to the maor.

title: Seann-chunntas
body: Tuathaich speakers begin to name the tabled request to the library and the dead motion for amends together as 'seann-chunntas', an old reckoning that none in power will settle and none has cancelled. The Dia-thìrich in office do not take up the word.

title: The Sloc Mòr closed
body: The Mine Board shuts the upper galleries of the Sloc Mòr at Achadh dhomhain. One face is kept open in the Rite's keeping, to cut coal for the altars, a few baskets a year.

title: The last hewers
body: Twelve hewers are kept at the Sloc Mòr to cut the altar-coal in the Rite's keeping. They are the last of their trade to work the vein on the island, and the Rite gives them its own oath, not the dissolved guild's.

title: The regiments at the Còmhrag
body: Fighters of the regiments are entered in the Còmhrag at Ceann leathan for the first time. The ninth regiment's man wins it. The fair-wardens raise the gate-price again.

title: The second regiment's library guard
body: The second regiment at Àth dhìreach keeps a guard at Leabharlann Muileann chaol over the sealed war archive. The keeper, Raghnall mac Mhuirich, writes to the council that the library did not ask for one.

title: The coal line carries no coal
body: The last coal train runs from Achadh dhomhain to Cathair dhearg. The coal line keeps its name and carries dubhan, wool and soldiers.

title: The sixth regiment on the northern road
body: The sixth regiment at Cnoc bheag keeps posts on the northern road where the boundary stones stand. For the first time since the Severance the Tuathaich going south must show a pass. The council's minute calls the passes for a time only.

title: The fair of the present year
body: The fair at Muileann òg draws traders from every shire the state holds. Tuathaich wool is sold there on its northern day, through Dia-thìrich factors, as it has been since the first fair.

title: The Còmhrag of the present year
body: The Còmhrag at Ceann leathan is fought with staves and fists, as it has been since edged tools were banned. Two regiments and nine shires send fighters. One man dies.

title: The eleven books
body: Ellen Marsh's eleven books are copied by hand in the Tuathaich schools and kept in the north. The library's catalogue lists the tabled request, and not the books.

title: The Moot of the present year
body: The Moot at Caol mhòr meets under Peter Hale. Its minute-books run unbroken from Walter Hale's first meeting. It has no standing in Dia-thìrich law and has never asked for any.

title: The dubhan works of the present
body: Dubhan is made at Seann Skell on the southern coast and at works in the east and north. Every lamp, engine, ship and lorry on the island runs on it. The coin is pegged to it, and the tithe is taken on every sale.

title: The Treasury's roll of the present year
body: The Treasury's roll for the year stands at 9,568 purses: 6,375 from the head-due, taken at eighteen purses on every five thousand heads, and 3,193 from the market-due, taken at seventeen in the hundred on every sale. The wartime tithe is carried on its own line under the regiments' pay. The windy coast pays neither due.

title: Dubhan's charter of export
body: Dubhan, who made the first working fuel and is now in his sixty-ninth year, wins from the council at Cathair dhearg, after a year of letters and three sittings, leave to sell dubhan beyond the island. It is the first leave the kingdom has given since the Severance for any good of Dia-thìr to pass beyond its waters. The charter is narrow. The Treasury sets each year's measure. The fuel is loaded only at Ros dhomhain, where a clerk of the Treasury takes the tithe on every barrel. The kingdom's depots and the Moot's are served first. Nothing of the vein goes with it: the vein's coal is not sold, and the custodians of Òrd Bhrìde seal every hold. Dubhan has told neither the council nor the chronicler who buys from him. In the autumn the first tank-hull loaded under the charter goes out past the north-western capes, and on the day she sails the priests of Manannan at Seann Skell say their prayer to keep the sea shut.

title: The altar-coal
body: The Rite's twelve hewers at the Sloc Mòr cut the year's altar-coal. It fills four baskets. The high custodian at Seann Skell shares it among the houses of the Rite by lot.

title: The chronicler's note on the present
body: Sìleas nic Rath writes at the foot of the year that the kingdom's record is whole in every part but two: the war, which is sealed, and the north, which was not asked.

title: The present
body: The coal is all but gone. The trade of the island runs on a name that once belonged to one man. The Dia-thìrich hold the capital and the sea. The Tuathaich hold the north, a grievance five years old, their Church, and the memory of the First Canoe, Naomh Breandan's voyage to the Isle of the Blessed, which the people who have twice defeated them still call folklore.
